title: Trains
strapline: Through the tunnel, over the bridge, all aboard — tracks, timetables and journeys that always join up.
intent: Solve real spatial problems: a track only works when the curves, straights and junctions fit — and close the loop.
Load up on prepositions — through the tunnel, over the bridge, under the arch, between the platforms — the train layout is a preposition machine.
Practise sequence and routine: journeys have an order — first stop, next stop, last stop — and timetables say what comes next.
Share a resource that genuinely must be shared: there is one track, favourite engines are finite, and the junction belongs to everyone.
Connect to the real railway on our doorstep — the station down the road, the tube, the trains children ride with their families.
implementation: Let children battle the track problem before helping — a loop that won't close is the best puzzle in the room; offer a curve, not a solution.
Commentate journeys with deliberate prepositions: 'through the tunnel, over the bridge, and now you're coming in between the platforms'.
Run the railway: name the stations after children, call out stops in order, and ask what the next station is before you get there.
Give the network jobs — mail to deliver, passengers to collect, coal to the power station — so journeys have purpose.
Use the junction as a turn-taking teacher: signals, a 'wait here' sign, and language for negotiating whose train passes first.
Add tickets, timetables and station signs for mark-making that the play actually needs.
Talk about children's real journeys — who came by tube today? — and rebuild them in track.
key_questions: The loop won't close — which piece do we need to fix it?
What's the next station, and who is waiting there?
Two trains have met at the junction — who should go first, and how do we decide?
How many carriages can your engine pull before it's too heavy?
Where does the tunnel go — and what might your train see inside?

impact.text: Children fit curves, straights and junctions together to close the loop, turning and swapping pieces until the track joins up.
Children use prepositions constantly as they drive — through the tunnel, over the bridge, under the arch, between the platforms.
Children count carriages onto their engine and match one passenger to each seat before the train may leave.
Children take turns at the junction and share out engines and track, increasingly settling disputes with words and signals first.
Children connect couplings and slot track pins with careful, controlled fingers, lining carriages up precisely.
Children narrate the railway as they run it — 'all aboard!', delays, lost tickets, the mail that must get through — using railway words like platform, signal and junction.
Children talk about real trains from their own lives — the station down the road, the tube with Dad — and rebuild those journeys in track.
Children call the stations in a fixed order on the repeated circuit and predict which stop comes next before the train arrives.

enhancements: A ticket office: hole punch, paper tickets, a money tin and a departures board for children to run.
Station name-signs — including the children's own real local station — and a simple picture timetable.
Boxes and tubes for engineering new tunnels and bridges the track must fit through.
Freight jobs: parcels, 'coal' (pom-poms) and a mail sack that must reach the last station by tidy-up.
A signal you can actually switch — red and green — to run the junction fairly.
Photos from a walk to the real station: the platform, the departure boards, the driver who waved.
A track-problem card: a photo of a broken loop for children to diagnose — which piece is missing?

playing_exploring: Every new layout is an experiment — what happens if the bridge goes here and the junction there?
Children replay their own real journeys, mixing memory into the play.
active_learning: The unclosed loop is a problem children refuse to abandon — they swap pieces until it joins.
Delivering the mail to the last station means completing the whole circuit, stop by stop.
creating_thinking: Children predict which piece will close the gap — curve or straight? — and check by trying.
Two drivers, one junction: children invent their own signal rules and hold each other to them.
